newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislators call on China to free Wang Dan.
newsitem.headline: HK legislators call on China to free Wang Dan.

text.p: Hong Kong legislators on Wednesday called on China to immediately free jailed dissident Wang Dan.
Legislators voted 29 to 26 in favour of the motion proposed by Ho Chun-yan of the Democratic Party, the largest party in the British colony's Legislative Council, after a three-hour debate.
Beijing has sidelined the party, a vocal critic of Chinese policies, from the power structures that it is crafting to run the territory after China resumes control at midnight on June 30 1997.

The debate sparked criticism from pro-China legislators and analysts said the motion was likely to attract an angry response from China, which rejects all criticism of its human rights record and its harsh punishment of dissenters.
A pro-Beijing legislator told the legislature that the debate was an interference in China's internal affairs.

"The trial of anyone on the mainland is an internal affair of China and outside the scope of the Hong Kong legislature now or in the future," said David Chu, who is also a member of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee which is overseeing the handover.

Wang, a former student leader involved in the 1989 democracy movement, was imprisoned for 11 years last week in Beijing on charges of plotting to overthrow the government after writing articles critical of China's communist government.

Democratic Party leader, lawyer Martin Lee, said Wang's imprisonment was cause for alarm in free-wheeling Hong Kong, which reverts to China in 237 days. China plans to scrap the legislature and install an appointed "provisional legislature" excluding Lee's party next July 1.
"A new fully appointed legislature will pass repressive laws as directed by Beijing," Lee wrote in an article on Wednesday.

He said Hong Kong faced a situation similar to that when dictator Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany and changed the laws through his control of the legislature, forcing German judges to pass judgements that inflicted grave injustices.
"There is good reason to fear that history will be repeated in Hong Kong," his article in the South China Morning Post said.
"The demise of our elected legislature will mean China's definition of subversion will be applied through our courts," Lee wrote.

"Today I am free to write commentaries in this and other newspapers ... It is a liberty my party members and I frequently exercise. But there is good reason to question whether I or anyone else will be able to exercise this freedom of expression after 1997," he added.
"As we debate the motion ... I will think one thing: today, Wang Dan. Tomorrow, you and me."
